nodes.description: In the mouse brain, loss of LGI3 alters short-term synaptic plasticity that depends on Kv1 channels, reducing short-term depression at callosal synapses onto layer 5 pyramidal neurons. This is the proposed central counterpart of the peripheral defect and a candidate cause of the intellectual disability, but Lgi3-null mice showed no behavioural deficit and no study has connected it to cognition in patients.

nodes.description: Lgi3-null mice have reduced and mislocalized Kv1 channel complexes in myelinated peripheral axons, with normal myelination. In the brain, loss of Lgi3 disrupts juxtaparanodal ADAM23 and Kv1 clustering and alters Kv1-mediated short-term synaptic plasticity. The mice develop normally and showed no behavioural deficit on rotarod, Morris water maze or IntelliCage testing, and myokymia has not been reported in them.

nodes.description: LGI3 accumulates at the juxtaparanodes of myelinated axons, where it binds the axonal receptor ADAM23 and co-assembles with Kv1 channel complexes. ADAM23 needs its LGI ligands to cluster those complexes; LGI2 can partly substitute for LGI3 in the peripheral nerve. The source of LGI3 differs by compartment: oligodendrocytes in the brain, and in peripheral nerve mainly the neurons themselves, acting in an autocrine fashion, rather than Schwann cells.

nodes.description: Motor axons fire spontaneously and repetitively, seen clinically as facial myokymia and electrically as signs of motor nerve instability. How mislocalized juxtaparanodal Kv1 channels produce this is not established: in mice their loss lengthens the refractory period rather than raising excitability, and no Lgi3 mutant mouse has been shown to have myokymia.
